blocks.text: The earlier Multi Agent Systems lesson looked at a planner, a researcher, and a writer working in a chain, one after another, with an orchestrator deciding who goes next.
Collaboration is a different pattern. Here, agents work on overlapping parts of the same task at roughly the same time, instead of waiting in a strict line.
This lesson covers splitting one task into parallel subtasks, running agents on them together, merging their results into one answer, and handling it when two agents disagree.
1. Collaboration Versus a Strict Hierarchy
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441305941-839826008.png
In a strict hierarchy, one agent finishes its piece before the next one starts, and each agent only sees the piece meant for it.
In collaboration, several agents can look at the same shared task at the same time, each covering a different angle of it.
Think of two people editing the same document at once instead of passing it down a line, one writer after another.

items: Hierarchy: planner then researcher then writer, one finishes before the next begins.
Collaboration: several agents work on overlapping parts of one task together, at the same time.
Hierarchy suits work that has a natural order. Collaboration suits work that can be split sideways.

blocks.text: 2. When Collaboration Actually Helps
Collaboration pays off when a task has parts that do not depend on each other, so agents are not stuck waiting on one another.
Summarizing three different articles into one combined summary is a good fit, since each article can be read on its own.
A task where step two truly needs step one's exact output is a poor fit, because parallel agents would just be guessing at each other's work.

blocks.title: Quick check
blocks.content: Ask whether two people could do the two halves of the task without talking to each other first. If yes, it is a good candidate for collaboration.

blocks.text: 3. Splitting a Task Into Subtasks
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441305943-310815518.png
The first real step in collaboration is deciding how to cut the task into pieces that make sense on their own.
A useful split gives each agent a subtask it can finish without needing to ask another agent a question mid way through.
A common approach is to split by topic, by section, by data source, or by a fixed list of items to check.

items: Split by section, one agent per section of a long document.
Split by source, one agent per input file, feed, or dataset.
Split by check, one agent per rule when validating something against several rules at once.

5. Running the Agents at the Same Time

blocks.alt: Running the Agents at the Same Time
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441305944-182250228.png
Once the subtasks exist, each one is handed to its own agent call, and those calls run at the same time instead of one after another.
Running calls concurrently mostly matters for speed, since three agents working together can finish close to as fast as the slowest single one.
It also means the agents genuinely do not see each other's output while working, which is exactly the collaboration pattern we want here.
6. A Concurrent Agent Call in Code
This example uses asyncio to fire off one simulated agent call per subtask, and waits for all of them together.

code.content:
import asyncio


async def run_agent(subtask):
    """Pretend agent call that scores the sentiment of one review."""
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)  # stands in for a real model call
    text = subtask["review_text"].lower()
    if "great" in text or "fast" in text:
        sentiment = "positive"
    elif "dented" in text or "scratches" in text:
        sentiment = "mixed"
    else:
        sentiment = "neutral"
    return {"subtask_id": subtask["subtask_id"], "sentiment": sentiment}


async def run_all(subtasks):
    calls = [run_agent(task) for task in subtasks]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*calls)
    return results


results = asyncio.run(run_all(subtasks))
print(results)

blocks.text: 7. What Merging Actually Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441305944-443085320.png
Merging is the step where the separate agent results get combined into one answer that reads as if a single voice wrote it.
This is more than pasting results one after another. It usually means summarizing, ordering, and removing repeated points.
A good merge step hides the seams between agents, so the reader never notices that three different calls produced the final text.

9. Checking Whether Results Agree
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441305945-460057874.png
Before trusting a merge, it helps to check whether the individual agent results actually line up with each other.
Two agents scoring the same review, or covering the same fact from two angles, should usually reach a similar conclusion.
10. Why Agents Disagree
Two agents can read the same input and land on different answers because language is genuinely ambiguous, not just because something is broken.
Different prompts, different amounts of context, or plain randomness in the model call can all push two agents toward different conclusions.
Disagreement is normal in collaboration, and the system needs a plan for it rather than hoping it never happens.
11. Handling Disagreement Between Agents
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441305945-87383756.png
The most common fix is a small judge step, a third call that looks at both conflicting answers and picks or blends one.
Another option is to simply rerun the disagreeing subtask and see if the new answer matches either of the first two.
A third option is to flag the conflict for a person to look at, which is often the safest choice for anything high stakes.

items: Judge step: a separate call compares the conflicting answers and picks the stronger one.
Rerun: redo the disagreeing subtask and see which earlier answer it matches.
Escalate: flag the conflict for a human reviewer instead of guessing automatically.

blocks.text: 14. Costs and Tradeoffs to Keep in Mind
Running several agents at once usually costs more, since every subtask is its own model call happening in the same window of time.
It also adds the extra work of merging and checking for conflicts, which a pure hierarchy does not need.
The tradeoff is worth it when the speed gain and the quality of a merged, cross checked answer outweigh the extra calls.
15. Giving Agents a Shared Context Store

blocks.alt: Giving Agents a Shared Context Store
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441305946-275852340.png
Even though agents work on separate subtasks, it often helps for them to read from one shared store, so no two agents waste effort on the same piece by accident.
A shared store can be as simple as a dictionary keyed by subtask id, holding what each agent has already found or decided.
This is different from the task state used in a hierarchy, since here several agents may read the same store at once instead of one agent handing off to the next.
16. Logging and Tracing Parallel Agent Calls
When several agents run at the same time, plain logging gets confusing fast, since messages from different calls can interleave.
Tagging every log line with a subtask id makes it possible to follow one agent's work even when three of them are printing output at once.
Recording how long each agent call took also helps later, when deciding whether parallel work is actually saving time.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.content: Give every subtask a short unique id at split time, and pass that id through logging, results, and the merge step, so any output can be traced back to its source.

blocks.text: 17. Deciding How Many Agents to Run at Once
Splitting a task into ten subtasks does not always mean running ten agents at the exact same moment.
A sensible limit on how many calls run in parallel keeps cost and load predictable, even when the total number of subtasks is large.
A common pattern is to process subtasks in small batches, running a handful of agents at once rather than every agent at once.

items: Small fan out, three to five agents at once, keeps cost and debugging manageable.
Large fan out speeds things up but makes conflicts and cost spikes more likely.
Batching subtasks lets you get most of the speed benefit while keeping the width under control.

blocks.text: Worked Example: Reviewing a Bug Report From Three Angles
Say the task is, review one bug report and decide if it is a real bug, a duplicate, or a feature request.
The task is split into three subtasks: one agent checks it against known bugs, one checks it against the feature list, and one just reads it for clarity.
All three agents run at the same time, each returning its own verdict on the same bug report.
The duplicate checker says duplicate, but the clarity reader says real bug, since the wording looked different from the known bug.
A judge step compares both verdicts, notices the underlying issue is the same as a known bug, and merges them into one final answer, duplicate, with a note explaining the different wording.
Common Mistakes

items: Splitting a task into subtasks that secretly depend on each other, so parallel agents end up guessing.
Merging results by simply concatenating them, instead of actually reconciling and summarizing.
Never checking whether two agents agree before treating the merged answer as final.
Treating every disagreement the same way, instead of picking judge, rerun, or escalate based on how serious the task is.
Running agents in parallel purely for speed, on a task that was never actually independent to begin with.

blocks.text: Practice
Take a short list of five customer comments and split them into five subtasks, one comment per agent.
Write a small script that runs all five agent calls at the same time and merges the results into one summary sentence.

items: Stretch goal one: have two of the five comments deliberately produce conflicting sentiment labels, then add a judge step to resolve it.
Stretch goal two: time your parallel version against a version that runs the same five calls one after another, and compare.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
Collaboration means splitting one task into independent subtasks, running agents on them at the same time, and merging their results into one coherent answer.
The extra piece collaboration needs that a strict hierarchy does not is a real plan for disagreement, whether that is a judge step, a rerun, or a human check.
